CHAPTER 7 · LEARNING AREA 7 · DECEMBER

Inferential statistics

On election night a forecast is fixed at 6 pm, although not a single vote has been counted: it is based on asking a few thousand voters. A baker is said to bake too many rolls that are too small, a coin is said to be biased. In this chapter you draw conclusions from a sample about the whole: you estimate proportions, means and variances and decide with significance tests whether a result is still chance or already evidence.

15 LESSONS3 UNITS4 WIDGETS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • the basic problems of inferential statistics: drawing conclusions from the sample about the population
  • calculate proportions, the sample mean and the sample variance and extrapolate them
  • set up and carry out one-tailed significance tests for binomially distributed random variables
  • carry out two-tailed tests and interpret what “significant” means and what it does not
  • for large $n$, approximate rejection regions with the normal distribution and check them with exact values

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1Basic problems and estimating parameters

Of $1200$ randomly chosen voters, $444$ want to vote for party A, that is $37\%$. Nobody knows whether it will be exactly $37\%$ in the election: another sample would have given a slightly different result. Inferential statistics asks what you can nevertheless say reliably from the sample.

The population is all voters, the sample is the part asked at random. Unknown key figures of the population (its parameters) are estimated by the corresponding key figures of the sample: the proportion $p$ by the relative frequency $h$, the mean $\mu$ by the sample mean $\bar x$, the variance $\sigma^2$ by the sample variance $s^2$. So that $s^2$ is right on average, you divide by $n - 1$.

Estimates vary from sample to sample. For proportions, $h$ spreads by about $\sqrt{\tfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$: you need four times the sample size for half the spread.

KEY POINT · ESTIMATING FROM A SAMPLE

Proportion: $p \approx h = \tfrac{k}{n}$ ($k$ hits among $n$) · Extrapolation: number in the population $\approx N \cdot h$

Sample mean: $\bar x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + \ldots + x_n}{n}$ · Sample variance: $s^2 = \dfrac{1}{n - 1} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar x)^2$, $s = \sqrt{s^2}$

The sample must be drawn at random, otherwise its estimates are systematically wrong.

Why $n - 1$? The values always spread a little less about their own mean $\bar x$ than about the true mean $\mu$. The factor $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$ makes up for this. The widget shows it with a thousand samples.

On election night the institutes extrapolate from the first polling districts counted. Choosing these districts well is the real art.

INTERACTIVE · ESTIMATING MEAN AND VARIANCE

A machine fills bottles. Draw samples and compare $\bar x$ with the target value. With “+1000” you see that $s^2$ with $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$ hits the true variance on average, but with $\tfrac1n$ comes out too small.

INTERACTIVE · PROPORTIONS VARY

Many samples from the same population: the relative frequencies spread around the true proportion $p$. Multiply $n$ by four and watch the width.

EXAMPLE 1 · FILL QUANTITIES

Five bottles contain $498$, $503$, $501$, $497$ and $501$ ml. Estimate the mean and the standard deviation of the filling.

$\bar x = \tfrac{2500}{5} = 500$ ml. Deviations $-2$, $3$, $1$, $-3$, $1$, squares $4 + 9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 24$.

$s^2 = \tfrac{24}{4} = 6$: $s \approx 2.45$ ml

EXAMPLE 2 · EXTRAPOLATION

Of $500$ parts tested, $12$ are faulty. How many faulty parts can be expected in a day's production of $20{,}000$ pieces?

$h = \tfrac{12}{500} = 0.024$, so $20{,}000 \cdot 0.024 = 480$.

About $480$ parts. The estimate spreads by about $\sqrt{\tfrac{0.024 \cdot 0.976}{500}} \approx 0.007$, that is by roughly $140$ parts.

EXERCISES

Calculate $\bar x$, $s^2$ and $s$ for the sample $3$, $7$, $5$, $9$, $6$.

$\bar x = 6$; deviations $-3$, $1$, $-1$, $3$, $0$, sum of squares $20$: $s^2 = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5$, $s \approx 2.24$.

Of $1200$ people asked, $444$ want to vote for party A. Estimate the proportion and extrapolate to $60{,}000$ voters.

$h = 0.37$; about $22{,}200$ votes.

For a survey on satisfaction with buses and trains, only people at a bus stop are asked. Why is this not a good sample?

The sample is not random: almost everyone at the bus stop takes the bus. Anyone who finds the service so bad that they take the car is hardly ever asked.

For the values $1$ and $3$, calculate the variance once with the factor $\tfrac1n$ and once with $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$. Which estimate is meant for a sample?

$\bar x = 2$, sum of squares $2$: with $\tfrac1n$ you get $1$, with $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$ you get $2$. For samples you use $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$.

How large must a survey be at least so that the spread $\sqrt{\tfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}$ of the estimated proportion is at most one percentage point for $p \approx 0.5$?

$\sqrt{\tfrac{0.25}{n}} \le 0.01$, so $\tfrac{0.25}{n} \le 0.0001$: $n \ge 2500$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$\tfrac{24}{4}$

$12$ out of $500$ faulty: extrapolation to $20{,}000$ pieces?

$20{,}000 \cdot 0.024$

How does the spread of an estimated proportion change if you multiply $n$ by four?

$\sqrt{4} = 2$ in the denominator

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2One-tailed significance tests

A baker says: at most $10\%$ of my rolls are too small. A customer suspects more and weighs $50$ rolls. Even if the baker is right, there may be more than $5$ rolls that are too small, by chance. From how many on may she contradict him without being wrong too often? She has to fix the rule for this before she weighs.

You test the null hypothesis $H_0\colon p = 0.1$ against the suspicion $H_1\colon p > 0.1$. The test statistic $X$ counts the rolls that are too small. If $H_0$ is true, $X$ is binomially distributed with $n = 50$ and $p = 0.1$. Large values of $X$ speak against $H_0$: the rejection region lies on the right. You choose it so that, if $H_0$ is true, it is hit with a probability of at most $\alpha$, the significance level.

A test can go wrong in two ways: $H_0$ is rejected although it is true (type I error, at most $\alpha$), or $H_0$ is kept although it is false (type II error).

KEY POINT · ONE-TAILED SIGNIFICANCE TEST

1. Fix $H_0\colon p = p_0$ and the direction. 2. Test statistic $X$, under $H_0$ binomially distributed with $n$ and $p_0$. 3. Choose the significance level $\alpha$.

4. Right-tailed: $K = \{k, \ldots, n\}$ with the smallest $k$ for which $P(X \ge k) \le \alpha$. Left-tailed: $K = \{0, \ldots, k\}$ with the largest $k$ for which $P(X \le k) \le \alpha$. $k$ is called the critical value.

5. Decision rule: if the sample result lies in $K$, $H_0$ is rejected, otherwise not.

Not rejected does not mean proved: if the result is not in $K$, the data are simply not enough to refute $H_0$.

On the calculator: many devices only know $P(X \le k)$. Then $P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k - 1)$.

INTERACTIVE · THE SIGNIFICANCE TEST

Set $n$, $p_0$, the direction and $\alpha$. Red is the rejection region. Switch on the type II error and change the true $p$: how often does the test miss that $H_0$ is false?

EXAMPLE 3 · RIGHT-TAILED: THE BAKER

$n = 50$, $H_0\colon p = 0.1$, $H_1\colon p > 0.1$, $\alpha = 5\%$. We have $P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.058$ and $P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.025$. The customer finds $9$ rolls that are too small.

$k = 9$ is too small ($0.058 > 0.05$), $k = 10$ works: $K = \{10, \ldots, 50\}$.

$9$ is not in $K$: $H_0$ is not rejected. The data are not enough to contradict the baker.

EXAMPLE 4 · LEFT-TAILED: THE SEEDS

A dealer promises that at least $90\%$ of the seeds germinate. A gardener sows $100$ seeds. $H_0\colon p = 0.9$, $H_1\colon p < 0.9$, $\alpha = 5\%$, with $P(X \le 84) \approx 0.040$ and $P(X \le 85) \approx 0.073$.

The rejection region lies on the left: the largest $k$ with $P(X \le k) \le 0.05$ is $84$.

$K = \{0, \ldots, 84\}$: if at most $84$ seeds germinate, the gardener contradicts the dealer.

EXERCISES

State $H_0$, $H_1$ and the type of test. a) A new medicine is supposed to work better than the old one with a cure rate of $70\%$. b) A supplier guarantees at most $3\%$ defective parts, the buyer has doubts. c) A party claims to have at least $30\%$ support.

a) $H_0\colon p = 0.7$, $H_1\colon p > 0.7$, right-tailed   b) $H_0\colon p = 0.03$, $H_1\colon p > 0.03$, right-tailed   c) $H_0\colon p = 0.3$, $H_1\colon p < 0.3$, left-tailed

A coin is tossed $30$ times. A right-tailed test checks whether it shows tails too often: $H_0\colon p = 0.5$, $\alpha = 5\%$. We have $P(X \ge 19) \approx 0.100$ and $P(X \ge 20) \approx 0.049$. Find $K$.

$K = \{20, \ldots, 30\}$

In the baker's test ($K = \{10, \ldots, 50\}$), in truth $20\%$ of the rolls are too small. With what probability does the customer not notice? We have $P(X \le 9) \approx 0.444$ for $n = 50$, $p = 0.2$.

Type II error: the result is not in $K$, so $P(X \le 9) \approx 44\%$. Almost every second check misses the bad baker.

In the seed test, a) $86$ seeds, b) $83$ seeds germinate. State the decision in words each time.

a) $86 \notin K$: the dealer's claim is not rejected. b) $83 \in K$: at the $5\%$ level the result speaks significantly against a germination rate of $90\%$.

The customer now weighs $100$ rolls. For $n = 100$, $p = 0.1$ we have $P(X \ge 15) \approx 0.073$ and $P(X \ge 16) \approx 0.040$; for $p = 0.2$, $P(X \le 15) \approx 0.129$. Find $K$ and the type II error for $p = 0.2$. What does the larger sample size achieve?

$K = \{16, \ldots, 100\}$, type II error $\approx 13\%$ instead of $44\%$. More data make the test sharper, with the same $\alpha$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Critical value in the baker's test ($n = 50$, $\alpha = 5\%$)?

$P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.025$

Largest number in the rejection region of the seed test?

$P(X \le 84) \approx 0.040$

A type I error means …

Its probability is at most $\alpha$.

UNIT 35 LESSONS

3Two-tailed tests and statistical certainty

Is a coin fair? Too many tails are suspicious, but so are too few. The rejection region therefore consists of two parts, one on the left and one on the right. So that the test as a whole is wrong with a probability of at most $\alpha$, each side gets at most $\tfrac{\alpha}{2}$.

If $H_0$ is rejected, you say: the result is significant at the level $\alpha$. That only means: if $H_0$ were true, such an extreme result would rarely occur. It does not mean that $H_0$ is false with probability $1 - \alpha$, nor that the difference is large or important. How well a test detects a false hypothesis depends on the true $p$ and on the sample size.

KEY POINT · TWO-TAILED TEST

$H_0\colon p = p_0$, $H_1\colon p \neq p_0$. Rejection region $K = \{0, \ldots, k_l\} \cup \{k_r, \ldots, n\}$ with

the largest $k_l$ for which $P(X \le k_l) \le \tfrac{\alpha}{2}$, and the smallest $k_r$ for which $P(X \ge k_r) \le \tfrac{\alpha}{2}$.

Significant means: if $H_0$ were true, the result would have landed in $K$ with a probability of at most $\alpha$.

The direction matters: if you know beforehand in which direction you are looking, you test one-tailed and detect deviations in this direction more easily.

With the CAS: call up the table of the cumulative binomial distribution and read off the limits $k_l$ and $k_r$; the widget below calculates the same.

INTERACTIVE · CUMULATIVE BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION

Set $n = 100$ and $p = 0.5$ and choose $P(X \le k)$. Look for the largest $k$ for which the probability is at most $0.025$.

EXAMPLE 5 · IS THE COIN FAIR?

$n = 100$, $H_0\colon p = 0.5$, $H_1\colon p \neq 0.5$, $\alpha = 5\%$. We have $P(X \le 39) \approx 0.018$ and $P(X \le 40) \approx 0.028$.

Left: $k_l = 39$. Because of the symmetry, on the right $k_r = 61$.

$K = \{0, \ldots, 39\} \cup \{61, \ldots, 100\}$. The type I error is even only $2 \cdot 0.0176 \approx 3.5\%$.

EXAMPLE 6 · IF THE COIN IS BIASED

In truth the coin shows tails with $p = 0.6$. How likely is it that the test does not detect this?

Type II error: $P(40 \le X \le 60)$ for $p = 0.6$ $\approx 0.54$.

In more than half of the cases the coin goes undetected. For $p = 0.7$ it is only about $2\%$.

EXERCISES

Explain why the fairness of a coin is tested two-tailed, but the effectiveness of a new medicine one-tailed.

With the coin, deviations in both directions are suspicious. With the medicine, all that matters is whether it is better.

$n = 50$, $H_0\colon p = 0.5$, two-tailed, $\alpha = 5\%$. We have $P(X \le 17) \approx 0.016$ and $P(X \le 18) \approx 0.033$. Find $K$.

$k_l = 17$, by symmetry $k_r = 33$: $K = \{0, \ldots, 17\} \cup \{33, \ldots, 50\}$

A dice is rolled $120$ times and tested two-tailed for the probability of a six, $\alpha = 5\%$. We have $P(X \le 11) \approx 0.014$, $P(X \le 12) \approx 0.028$, $P(X \ge 28) \approx 0.037$, $P(X \ge 29) \approx 0.022$. Find $K$. What is the decision with $27$ sixes?

$K = \{0, \ldots, 11\} \cup \{29, \ldots, 120\}$. $27 \notin K$: $H_0$ is not rejected.

True or false? a) The result is significant, so $H_0$ is false with a probability of $95\%$. b) If $H_0$ is not rejected, it is proved. c) A smaller $\alpha$ makes the type II error larger.

a) false: $\alpha$ describes the behaviour of the test if $H_0$ is true, not a probability for $H_0$. b) false. c) true, the rejection region gets smaller.

A coin in truth has $p = 0.55$. In the two-tailed test with $\alpha = 5\%$ the type II error is about $0.86$ for $n = 100$ and about $0.52$ for $n = 400$. Interpret the numbers. What follows for planning a test?

Small deviations almost always go undetected with $100$ tosses, and even with $400$ in every second case. If you want to find small differences, you need very large samples; this has to be planned before the test.

With $\alpha = 5\%$, what is the largest probability each side of a two-tailed test may have?

Exercise 15

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A dice test with $60$ rolls has $K = \{16, \ldots, 60\}$. How many sixes do you expect with a fair dice? What is the decision with $14$ and with $18$ sixes?

Expected $10$. With $14$ do not reject, with $18$ reject: the dice shows a six significantly too often.

Connecting with Year 11: use Bernoulli's formula to calculate $P(X \ge 9)$ for $n = 10$ and $p = 0.5$. Would you consider a coin biased with $9$ hits out of $10$ ($\alpha = 5\%$, right-tailed)?

$P(X = 9) + P(X = 10) = \tfrac{10 + 1}{1024} \approx 0.011 \le 0.05$: yes, significant at the $5\%$ level.

Explain why the rejection region has to be fixed before the sample is drawn.

If you only set the limit after seeing the result, you can place it so that the verdict you want comes out. Then the statement about the type I error no longer holds.

A party used to have $40\%$. After a scandal, $200$ people are asked. Plan a test with which the party can check at $\alpha = 5\%$ whether its share has fallen. For $n = 200$, $p = 0.4$ the CAS gives $P(X \le 68) \approx 0.048$ and $P(X \le 69) \approx 0.064$.

Left-tailed, $H_0\colon p = 0.4$, $H_1\colon p < 0.4$, $K = \{0, \ldots, 68\}$. If at most $68$ of the $200$ people asked want to vote for the party, the fall is significant.

Connecting with chapter 6: a coin is tossed $1000$ times and tested two-tailed at $\alpha = 5\%$. Find the range in which $H_0\colon p = 0.5$ is kept, using $\mu \pm 1.96\sigma$. Check it with the CAS values $P(X \le 468) \approx 0.0231$ and $P(X \le 469) \approx 0.0268$.

$\mu = 500$, $\sigma \approx 15.81$, $1.96\sigma \approx 31$: kept for $469$ to $531$. Check: $P(X \le 468) \le 0.025$, but $P(X \le 469) > 0.025$, so $K = \{0, \ldots, 468\} \cup \{532, \ldots, 1000\}$ ✔ The approximation is spot on.

A bakery claims that at most $10\%$ of its rolls are too light. An inspector weighs $400$ rolls ($\alpha = 5\%$, right-tailed). Find the smallest number $k$ of rolls that are too light from which on she contradicts, first with the approximation $k \ge \mu + 1.645\,\sigma + 0.5$, then with $P(X \ge 50) \approx 0.060$ and $P(X \ge 51) \approx 0.044$.

$\mu = 40$, $\sigma = 6$: $k \ge 40 + 9.87 + 0.5 = 50.37$, so $k = 51$. Exactly: $P(X \ge 51) \le 0.05 < P(X \ge 50)$, $K = \{51, \ldots, 400\}$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The lady tasting tea

In 1935, in his book The Design of Experiments, the statistician Ronald A. Fisher described a famous experiment: a lady claims she can taste whether the milk or the tea was poured into the cup first. Eight cups are prepared, four of each kind, in random order. She has to pick out the four cups with the milk first.

If she only guesses, there are $\binom{8}{4} = 70$ equally likely choices, and only one is completely right: probability $\tfrac{1}{70} \approx 1.4\%$. So a faultless result is significant at the $5\%$ level. With just one mistake it would no longer be: you guess at least that well with a probability of $\tfrac{17}{70} \approx 24\%$. Incidentally, the lady is said to have really existed: according to a later report, the botanist Muriel Bristol identified all eight cups correctly.

Sources: R. A. Fisher, The Design of Experiments, 1935, chapter 2. The report on Muriel Bristol comes from H. Fairfield Smith, quoted in D. Salsburg, The Lady Tasting Tea, 2001.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

ESTIMATING

$p \approx h$, $\mu \approx \bar x$, $\sigma^2 \approx s^2 = \tfrac{1}{n-1} \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$

Fill quantities: $\bar x = 500$ ml, $s^2 = 6$

HYPOTHESES

$H_0\colon p = p_0$; $H_1$ gives the direction.

Baker: $H_0\colon p = 0.1$, $H_1\colon p > 0.1$

ONE-TAILED

$K$ on the right or on the left with $P(X \in K) \le \alpha$

$n = 50$: $K = \{10, \ldots, 50\}$

TWO-TAILED

at most $\tfrac{\alpha}{2}$ on each side

Coin, $n = 100$: $K = \{0, \ldots, 39\} \cup \{61, \ldots, 100\}$

ERRORS

Type I: $H_0$ wrongly rejected, at most $\alpha$; type II: $H_0$ wrongly kept

Coin with $p = 0.6$: type II error $\approx 54\%$
